content: Uterine malformations result from abnormal development of the Müllerian ducts during embryogenesis. These malformations can present with a range of symptoms, including amenorrhea, infertility, and pelvic pain, or they may not cause any noticeable symptoms, depending on the specific defect. Approximately 1% of the female population is affected by uterine malformations. Types of Uterine Malformations 1. Class I: Müllerian Agenesis (Absent Uterus) In this condition, the uterus is absent, and the vagina may be rudimentary or completely absent. This condition is also known as Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome. Patients with MRKH syndrome typically present with primary amenorrhea. 2. Class II: Unicornuate Uterus (One-Sided Uterus) Only one side of the Müllerian duct develops, resulting in a uterus with a characteristic banana shape on imaging studies. 3. Class III: Uterus Didelphys (Double Uterus) Both Müllerian ducts develop but fail to fuse, leading to the formation of two separate uteri. In some cases, the lower Müllerian system may fuse into a single structure. Rarely, women with uterus didelphys can experience spontaneous pregnancies in both uteri, as seen in cases of twin pregnancies in one uterus and a singleton in the other. 4. Class IV: Bicornuate Uterus (Uterus with Two Horns) The upper part of the Müllerian system fails to fuse, resulting in a uterus with a bifurcated cranial portion while the caudal portion remains normal. This condition gives the uterus a heart-shaped appearance. 5. Class V: Septate Uterus (Uterine Septum or Partition) The two Müllerian ducts fuse, but the partition between them persists, dividing the uterine cavity into two parts. A complete septum can also partition the vagina, cervix, and uterus. Typically, the septum affects only the cranial portion of the uterus. A uterine septum is the most common uterine malformation and is a known cause of recurrent miscarriages. Diagnosis is made using imaging techniques such as hysterosalpingography, ultrasound, or MRI. Surgical correction is possible through hysteroscopic surgery. 6. Class VI: DES Uterus The uterine cavity has a T-shape due to fetal exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES). Another variation is the arcuate uterus, characterized by a concave dimple in the uterine fundus within the cavity. A rudimentary uterus, which is an underdeveloped uterine remnant not connected to the cervix or vagina, may also be present, often on the opposite side of a unicornuate uterus. Patients with uterine abnormalities may also have associated renal anomalies, such as unilateral renal agenesis. Double Vagina Uterus didelphys is a rare malformation (occurring in approximately 1 in 1,000 women) in which some reproductive organs are split or duplicated. These additional structures are often non-functional or semi-functional, but in some cases, they may be fully functional and independent. Since the vagina is primarily derived from the Müllerian ducts, incomplete fusion of the ducts can result in a vaginal septum, or double vagina. This condition is sometimes associated with uterus didelphys or a uterine septum. Diagnosis In addition to a physical examination, imaging techniques are essential for diagnosing uterine malformations. These include gynecologic ultrasonography, pelvic MRI, and hysterosalpingography. In some cases, laparoscopy and/or hysteroscopy may be indicated. Vaginal development may also be affected in certain patients. Treatment Surgical intervention depends on the specific nature and extent of the malformation. For a didelphic uterus, surgery is generally not recommended unless there are significant symptoms or complications.
